cases.name: State v. Puloka
cases.summary: Failed all three gates: no model card or forensic-community validation (G1), no domain-specific error rate and unexplained training data (G2), no provenance record documenting enhancement transformations (G3). Topaz Video AI added 16× as many pixels as the original. Court found the technique novel, opaque, and likely to cause confusion.

requirements.why: Topaz Labs published no model card covering intended use, subgroup performance, or limitations for forensic enhancement.
The training data behind Topaz Video AI’s models was unknown to the expert who ran the enhancement.
Tool named only as “Topaz Video AI” by a video editor; no build number or configuration parameters were recorded.
No validation by the forensic video community — forensic analysts did not recognise the technique.
Proprietary algorithms; no source-code access was offered or available.
Low-resolution, compressed phone footage fell outside any validated input domain.
No error rate was offered for this input domain or task.
No version-specific validation — and the tool added roughly 16× the original pixels with no measure of fidelity.
No explainability output separating inferred pixels from recorded ones.
No provenance record documented the transformations between the source clip and the enhanced exhibit.
No hash chain linked the original recording to the enhanced output.
Enhancement settings and model parameters were not logged.
The enhancement could not be reproduced by an independent examiner.

cases.name: State v. Pickett
cases.summary: Gate 1 failure: insufficient disclosure of TrueAllele source code. Court held “without scrutinizing source code in an adversarial system, no finding of reliability could realistically be made.” Validation studies existed but were vendor-conducted.

requirements.why: TrueAllele’s limitations were not disclosed in a form the defense could test.
Validation datasets were described in vendor publications but not produced for independent review.
TrueAllele was identified as the tool used for the mixture interpretation.
Validation studies existed but were largely vendor-conducted or vendor-affiliated.
Source code was withheld until the court ordered disclosure under a protective order.
A complex, low-template mixture pushed the limits of the published validation.
Error rates were published for mixtures generally, not for this mixture profile.
No showing that validation covered the specific software version used.
A likelihood ratio was reported, but how it was reached could not be examined without the code.

g3.note: Not reached: the dispute centred on disclosure, and the chain of custody of the DNA data was not challenged.

cases.name: State v. Arteaga
cases.summary: Gate 1 and 2 failures: state had not disclosed FRT system details, probe image quality, candidate list, or error rates. Court grounded its order in Brady obligations and the right to impeach the investigation.

requirements.why: The State did not disclose the FRT system’s design, performance metrics, or limitations.
No information about the gallery database or training data was provided.
The system and version that generated the match were not identified.
No validation results were provided to the defense.
Not sought — the order targeted system details, error rates, and the candidate list.
Probe-image quality was undisclosed, so fit with a validated domain could not be assessed.
No error rates were disclosed.
No version-specific validation was offered.
The candidate list and any analyst edits to the probe image were withheld.

g3.note: Not reached: the court resolved the matter as a Brady discovery order before any provenance question arose.

cases.name: State v. Miles
cases.summary: Court affirmed minimum disclosure obligations but reversed source-code order without particularized need showing. Consistent with the framework’s proportionality principle.

requirements.why: Court required disclosure of basic system documentation and performance information.
Gallery database information was required only at a general level.
Minimum disclosure obligations included identifying the FRT system used.
Error-rate and testing information was required, but independent validation was not mandated.
Source-code order reversed absent a particularized showing of need — consistent with proportionality.
Probe-image characteristics were disclosed, but domain fit was not ruled on.
Available error rates were ordered disclosed; no domain-specific rate was required.
Version-specific validation was not addressed.
Explainability output was not addressed.

g3.note: Not reached: the ruling concerned pre-trial discovery, not admission of an FRT artifact.

cases.name: Mendones v. Cushman & Wakefield
cases.summary: Gate 3 failure: deepfake exhibits detected through metadata inconsistencies (iPhone 6 provenance claims for footage the device couldn’t produce). A provenance requirement would have caught fabrication before submission.

g1.note: Not reached: the exhibits were presented as ordinary recordings, so no AI tool was ever disclosed.

g2.note: Not reached: with no disclosed AI tool, there was no application whose reliability could be tested.

requirements.why: No provenance record; the claimed iPhone 6 origin was contradicted by the files’ own metadata.
No hash linked the exhibits to an original capture device.
Generation parameters were never logged because the AI origin was concealed.
The exhibits could not be traced to, or reproduced from, a genuine original recording.

cases.name: United States v. Williams
cases.summary: No gates applied. Investigator “disavowed any particular knowledge of [Cellebrite’s] technology.” Under the framework, interpretive functions within extraction suites would trigger Gates 1 and 2.

requirements.why: No documentation of Cellebrite’s analytic features was requested or offered.
No information on data used to build the tool’s parsing or categorisation features.
Extraction version and settings were not established by the testifying investigator.
No validation evidence offered; the investigator disavowed knowledge of the technology.
Source code was not sought.
No inquiry into whether the device and OS were supported by the extraction version.
No error rate for the tool’s parsing or categorisation functions.
Version-specific results were not examined.
The investigator could not explain how the tool produced its reports.
The extraction report was admitted without a machine-readable transformation log.
Hash verification of the extraction was never put at issue.
Not applicable — physical extraction is deterministic.
No showing that an independent examiner could reproduce the report.

cases.name: State v. Loomis
cases.summary: Court accepted proprietary COMPAS risk score at sentencing with warnings about proprietary nature and possible racial disparities, but did not require validation data or error rates. Under the framework, the interpretive scoring function would trigger all three gates.

requirements.why: Score accepted without documentation of COMPAS’s intended use or subgroup performance.
The norming population and training data were not disclosed.
The COMPAS version and configuration used were not examined.
No independent validation for the Wisconsin population was required.
Trade-secret protection meant the defendant could not examine the methodology.
No showing that COMPAS was validated for this population or for sentencing use.
No error rate required — the court only warned about possible racial disparities.
Version-specific results were not examined.
The score was delivered without any explanation of the factors driving it.

g3.note: Not reached: the integrity of the score’s computation was never placed in issue.

cases.name: Huang v. Tesla
cases.summary: Tesla claimed Musk videos might be deepfakes to avoid authentication. Judge found it “deeply troubling” and ordered Musk to testify under oath. Canonical rejection of the “liar’s dividend.” Provenance documentation would have resolved authentication immediately.

g1.note: Not reached: no AI tool was offered — Tesla only speculated that the videos might be deepfakes.

g2.note: Not reached: the question was authenticity of recordings, not reliability of an AI system.

requirements.why: No provenance record existed for the recordings, leaving room for the deepfake claim.
No hash chain connected the original recordings to the copies in circulation.
Not applicable — the recordings were not produced by a generative process.
Authenticity could be resolved only by ordering Musk to testify under oath.

cases.name: Kohls v. Ellison
cases.summary: Stanford AI expert’s declaration excluded after ChatGPT-generated fabricated citations discovered. Judge called it “ironic” that an AI misinformation expert fell victim to AI hallucinations. Failed Gate 1 (no verification) and Gate 2 (hallucinated sources destroyed reliability).

requirements.why: ChatGPT use in drafting the declaration was not disclosed, so no model documentation was before the court.
No training-data information — the model’s involvement was itself undisclosed.
The tool was identified only after the fabricated citations were exposed; no version or prompts were recorded.
No validation: AI-drafted text was never checked against the sources it cited.
Not at issue — the failure was undisclosed use, not a need to inspect the model.
Generating scholarly citations is a known LLM failure domain; output was used outside any validated task.
No error rate for hallucinated citations was considered or disclosed.
Hallucinated citations to non-existent articles appeared in the sworn declaration.
The expert could not explain how the AI produced the fabricated references.

g3.note: Not applicable: the declaration was excluded at Gates 1–2, and no AI-generated artifact was offered as evidence.

cases.name: Matter of Weber
cases.summary: Court excluded expert’s valuation as unreliable and speculative, noting reliance on generative AI. First published decision announcing an AI-disclosure duty for counsel.

requirements.why: The expert relied on Microsoft Copilot with no model documentation.
No training-data information was offered.
Copilot was named, but the expert could not say what prompts or inputs were used.
No validation of the AI-assisted calculations was offered.
Not at issue.
Financial valuation is outside any validated task for a general-purpose chatbot.
No error rate — and the court’s own Copilot queries returned differing figures.
Outputs could not be tied to a specific, validated run.
The expert could not explain how Copilot reached its figures.

g3.note: Not reached: the valuation was excluded at Gates 1–2, and no AI-generated exhibit was offered.

cases.name: Ferlito v. Harbor Freight
cases.summary: Court refused to exclude expert who used an LLM to double-check findings. Demonstrates that responsible, verified AI use by experts survives scrutiny — the AI was a check, not the source of the opinion.

requirements.why: Not required: the LLM served as a verification check, not the analytical source of the opinion.
Not material: the opinion did not rest on the LLM’s training data.
The expert disclosed using an LLM to double-check his findings.
AI served as a verification check — the conclusions came from the expert’s own methodology.
Not sought or required given the LLM’s limited role.
The expert’s underlying methodology was independently reliable.
No error rate needed: the LLM did not generate the opinion.
Not required for a confirmatory check.
The LLM did not alter the substance of the opinion, which the expert could fully explain.

g3.note: Not applicable: no AI-generated artifact was offered — the expert’s own opinion was the evidence.

cases.name: Schulte v. LinkedIn
cases.summary: First federal court to accept generative AI (Relativity aiR) making final responsiveness determinations in e-discovery. Court treated it as TAR under existing proportionality principles, not novel technology requiring new rules.

requirements.why: Relativity aiR’s use was disclosed under the parties’ ESI protocol.
Not required: performance was measured on the case’s own documents rather than through vendor training data.
Tool identified by name and version (Relativity aiR).
The review workflow and its validation approach were documented and shared.
Not sought — proportionality principles for e-discovery did not call for it.
Applied to its intended task, with the proportionality analysis under FRCP 26(b)(1) satisfied.
Quality-control sampling with human review measured performance for this review.
Validation results were tied to the review run actually performed.
Per-document rationales let human reviewers check each responsiveness call.
Documented pipeline from search terms through AI review to QC sampling.
Platform audit logs tracked documents across stages; formal hash verification was not at issue.
Review criteria and run configuration were recorded as part of the workflow.
The workflow was documented well enough to be re-run and audited.

cases.name: Simmons v. Ferrigno
cases.summary: Second Circuit found ShotSpotter relevant under Rule 401, authenticatable under Rule 901(a) through employee testimony, and not unfairly prejudicial. No formal validation framework required.

requirements.why: No model card for ShotSpotter’s classification algorithms.
Acoustic training data was not documented.
The system was identified and explained through ShotSpotter employee testimony.
The court accepted employee testimony on accuracy without independent validation.
Source code was not sought.
Alert conditions were described but not tested against validated conditions.
Vendor accuracy figures were offered; no domain-specific error rate.
Version-specific results were not examined.
An employee explained the alert and its human review in testimony.

g3.note: Not reached: authentication under Rule 901(a) through employee testimony was treated as sufficient.

cases.name: ShotSpotter/Chicago
cases.summary: Judge found ShotSpotter unreliable after evidence showed employees reclassified a “firecracker” alert as “gunshot” and changed the reported location by ~1 mile to match the police narrative.

requirements.why: Proprietary classification algorithms were not disclosed.
The classification methodology and its training data were not documented.
The sensor configuration and software version behind the alert were not specified.
No independent validation — reliance on vendor-funded studies.
Source code was withheld as a trade secret.
A dense urban acoustic environment was not shown to be within validated conditions.
No domain-specific error rate for telling gunshots from firecrackers.
An employee reclassified a “firecracker” alert as “gunshot”, so the output wasn’t the validated system’s result.
The reported location moved by about a mile with no explanation of how.
No immutable audit trail of the human edits to the alert.
No integrity checks — the altered classification replaced the original.
Reclassification criteria and reviewer actions were not logged.
The reclassification was discovered only through adversarial litigation, not from the record.

cases.name: Lipps wrongful detention
cases.summary: Angela Lipps arrested after Clearview AI facial recognition misidentified her as a fraud suspect. She spent over five months in jail before charges dropped. No gate scrutiny was applied before the arrest.

requirements.why: Clearview’s documentation was not consulted before the arrest.
The scraped image gallery behind the match was never examined.
No record of which search or version produced the lead.
No validation — the match was treated as an identification.
Not sought.
Probe-image quality was not assessed before relying on the match.
No error rate was considered for the match.
Version-specific results were not examined.
No similarity score or explanation was reviewed, and no corroboration sought.
No record linked the probe image, search, and candidate selection.
Integrity of the search output was not examined.
Search settings were not logged.
No independent examiner reproduced the match before the arrest.

cases.name: Wakefield / Gissantaner
cases.summary: TrueAllele (Frye) and STRmix (Daubert) respectively held admissible when properly validated. Shows probabilistic genotyping survives challenge when independent validation exists.

requirements.why: Developers published methodology, intended use, and limitations.
Validation datasets were described in peer-reviewed literature.
TrueAllele and STRmix were identified, with versions in the record.
Independent validation, including by forensic laboratories, supported reliability.
Source code was not produced in Wakefield; the court found validation sufficient without it.
The courts found the mixtures within validated contributor and template ranges.
Published error rates and likelihood-ratio performance data were available.
Validation covered the software versions used.
Likelihood ratios came with supporting diagnostics, though internal reasoning stays opaque.

g3.note: Not reached: the chain of custody of the DNA data and analysis was not contested.
